title: Romanesque style walk
premise: Rusticated stone, deeply recessed round arches and turrets: four Romanesque façades between Eighteenth Street and Twenty-first.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ROMANESQUE STYLE. A winter afternoon, 1904, with the elms leafless and the masonry exposed. During the 1880s a Boston architect, Henry Hobson Richardson, revived the prestige of massive masonry: rough-faced blocks, profound round arches evoking a castle gateway, and towers. Chicago embraced the idiom enthusiastically, and for several years its wealthy residents commissioned fortresses.

Four residences on foot, from 1800 to 2110 Prairie. Identify rock-faced stone, arches that appear to recede into the wall, and turrets.

Commence with the residence that inaugurated the fashion, the one its neighbors resented.

stops.text: 1800 Prairie, Glessner House, the avenue's original Richardsonian Romanesque composition. Its street elevations are brick veneered with alternating six- and eight-inch sheets of granite, cut deeper at the openings so the entire wall simulates monolithic stone, beneath a roof of unglazed red tiles. Richardson, all 370 pounds of him, maintained that the windows of an urban residence were "not to look out of", so the street elevation is nearly windowless while the family rooms open toward a courtyard behind. George Pullman, diagonally opposite, protested about "that thing staring me in the face". Across the avenue and slightly south, the idiom acquired imitators.

1811 Prairie, the Coleman residence of 1886, designed by Cobb and Frost, architects distinguished for their Romanesque commissions. This façade is rough-faced brown sandstone. The 1888 plate displays the idiom's signature composition: a profound round arch on clustered columns surmounting a broad stair, with a corbelled oriel projecting above it like a sentinel's lookout on a castle rampart. Observe that the arch constitutes the entrance itself: in this idiom, entering becomes a passage tunneled into the masonry. Walk south beyond Twentieth Street for two smaller fortresses.

2011 Prairie, a neighbor of the Mayer residence. The district register classifies it as Romanesque: a rough ashlar façade, a round-arched entrance, and a rounded corner turret beneath a conical cap. A turret on an urban lot is essentially theatrical, a defensive tower grafted incongruously onto a townhouse. Across the avenue and one block farther, the final example compresses the idiom onto a single narrow lot.

2110 Prairie, Harriet Rees's narrow residence, which the district register attributes to Cobb and Frost in 1888 and classifies as Romanesque: a limestone façade beneath a tall gable addressing the avenue. Two years after the Coleman residence, the identical architects interpreted the idiom in pale stone for a woman's household. Compare the two compositions: the same firm, employing opposite palettes.

legs.story: Across the avenue and onward to the 2100 block.

endings.text:
The Romanesque walk concludes here. Rusticated stone, round arches and towers characterized the architectural fashion of the 1880s on this avenue.

Nevertheless Richardson's fortress outlived virtually every residence surrounding it, and it remains standing. Walk back to Eighteenth Street and examine it once more in the winter illumination.

keepsake.title: Romanesque field note
keepsake.text: A modern field note documenting the idiom's characteristic features; not a period document.

evidence.text: Joseph G. Coleman Residence. Built 1886; Cobb & Frost, architects. Cobb & Frost were well known for their designs in the Romanesque style, executed here in rough-faced brown sandstone.
The 1888 plate shows a rock-faced brown-stone front with a deep round arch on clustered columns over a broad stair, and a corbelled oriel over the arch.
evidence.locator: The whole plate: the street front and south flank from the roadway south-west of the house.

evidence.text: Glessner describes unglazed red roof tiles and granite street walls as part of the house's construction.
evidence.locator: HABS transcription, data pages 13-15; construction description, not the 1923 garage conversion.

evidence.text: John Glessner Residence. Built 1887; Henry Hobson Richardson, architect. Designed in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, the house is wrapped around a spacious light-filled courtyard.
The district draft reads 2011 Prairie from the T-1837 register as Romanesque: a rough ashlar front, a round-arched entrance and a rounded corner turret under a conical cap.

The district draft reads the Harriet Rees house (Cobb & Frost, 1888) from the T-1837 register as Romanesque: a limestone front under a tall gable facing the avenue; its carved tympanum, loggia and bowed oriel are later refinements.
The route, its order, its winter afternoon, its reading times, its keepsake and its framing are modern interpretation; no historical visit, conversation or occupant on a day in 1904 is asserted.
Glessner remembered Richardson weighing three hundred and seventy pounds: 'big-minded, big-bodied, big-hearted'.
Richardson held that the windows of a city house were 'not to look out of', since people shroud them in shades and curtains.
The street walls are brick faced with alternately six- and eight-inch sheets of granite, with deeper slabs returned at the openings to imply a wall entirely of stone.
evidence.locator: Data page 21, Part II.B.2, Wall construction.

evidence.text: George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.
